The core mechanism of sign-gestalt fixation arises from a shift in probabilistic decision-making where initial cognitive flexibility (docile sign-gestalt) degenerates into rigid adherence (mechanical attachment). This transition can be formalized through a Markovian model where transition probabilities P(s_i → s_j) depend on prior success history. As the animal accumulates evidence favoring one action (e.g., right-hand alley), the probability distribution shifts toward a peak at that action, eventually becoming a fixed point. The emergence of position-habit exemplifies this by showing how repeated reinforcement leads to a stable attractor in policy space, even when external cues suggest otherwise. Delayed reaction further complicates this by introducing a temporal dimension where immediate feedback is insufficient to update beliefs quickly enough. In GSI, this manifests as Bayesian belief drift under delayed observation; in GSE, it appears as persistent state transitions that resist change until sufficient counter-evidence accumulates.
